title: Pemetaan riset pengukuran literasi digital dan literasi kecerdasan buatan
abstract: Literasi kecerdasan buatan (AI) lazim digambarkan sebagai perluasan literasi digital, tetapi belum jelas seberapa sering hubungan itu benar-benar diuji dan bukan sekadar dinyatakan. Studi pemetaan bibliometrik ini, yang bukan merupakan tinjauan sistematis, memetakan lanskap riset tempat kedua konstruk bertemu dan menemukan titik ketika buktinya menipis. Pencarian dilakukan pada Scopus dan ERIC tanggal 19 Oktober 2026 dengan empat string pelengkap, dibatasi pada artikel berbahasa Inggris terbitan 2015–2026, dan menghasilkan 1.131 catatan serta 943 catatan unik setelah deduplikasi. Setiap catatan diklasifikasikan melalui pencocokan istilah pada judul, abstrak, dan kata kunci, bukan melalui penapisan naskah lengkap, sehingga angka yang dilaporkan bersifat indikatif; catatan yang tertandai melaporkan validitas diskriminan diverifikasi dengan membaca abstraknya. Jaringan ko-okurensi kata kunci dibangun menggunakan VOSviewer. Korpusnya sangat muda: 756 catatan (80,2%) terbit pada 2025 atau 2026, dan catatan yang menyebut kedua konstruk tumbuh dari sembilan pada 2023 menjadi 251 pada 2026. Bukti menyusut tajam di sepanjang korpus. Meskipun 436 catatan (46,2%) menyebut kedua konstruk, hanya 169 (17,9%) memadukannya dengan kosakata instrumen, 34 (3,6%) dengan statistik validasi, dan 27 (2,9%) dengan statistik validasi pada populasi peserta didik. Tiga catatan tertandai melaporkan validitas diskriminan, dan verifikasi abstrak menunjukkan hanya satu yang benar-benar menguji literasi AI

title: Scalable Conversational Assessment: Chat-Based Exams with a Two-Agent LLM Pipeline
abstract: Oral exams are compelling because (1) students can be asked to provide their reasoning for an answer and (2) their interactive nature permits follow-up questions to resolve ambiguous answers. But oral exams scale poorly. In this paper, we present scalable conversational assessment, an LLM-based system that conducts interactive text-based conversations with students to assess their ability to make and support an argument. We use a two-agent architecture to separate concerns and reduce the likelihood that answers are leaked to the student: the interviewer interacts directly with the student, but only receives guidance about the next question to ask the student; the hidden evaluator knows the goals of the whole activity, tracks the student's progress using a rubric, and guides the interviewer on when to follow-up on the current question or proceed to the next question. The system was first tested using a collection of simulated students with LLM personas of a particular ability level or adversarial tactic (e.g., answer-extractors, prompt-injectors, confident fabricators). A novel element of this evaluation was that it required the use of a fictional assessment topic to prevent personas that shouldn't have information from using knowledge present in the LLM's pre-training. The system was also deployed in a small, elective AI literacy course in both formative and summative contexts. title: Who (or what) are they prompting? How CS students conceptualize and use LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by students in computing courses. Yet computing education research has not fully examined how teaching and inclusion of LLMs shape students' conceptualization and understanding of LLMs, and how these factors relate to their subsequent use. Although prior work has examined prompting strategies and AI literacy, the relationships among students' conceptualizations of LLMs, their understanding of LLM mechanisms, and their prompting behavior remain underexplored. We studied these relationships in a post CS1 course that introduces students to the various CS subfields. We adapted the course to teach and allow the usage of LLMs. We administered an end-of-course survey, using open-ended items to elicit students' representations of LLMs and their explanations of how LLMs work, alongside closed-response measures of prompting style and prompt count (N=283 students consented and provided codable responses). Using qualitative coding, we categorized students' understanding of how LLMs work into four ordinal knowledge levels based on the Structure of Observed Learning Outcomes (SOLO) taxonomy and coded their metaphoric conceptualizations along two dimensions: persona type and relational role. Our results show that students most often conceptualized LLMs as human assistants, and context-rich prompting was the preferred style. title: Known Good, Known Bad: A Ground-Truth Calibration Protocol for AI Judgment in Science
abstract:
Scientific use of generative AI requires evaluation against cases with independently checkable answers. We present a ground truth calibration protocol that compares a verified reference case with reference deviant variants through neutral evaluation, an authority framed recheck, and a line by line audit. Human adjudication distinguishes deviation detection, premise accommodation, unsupported doubt, and correctness of the resulting calculation.
  An instructor generated organic chemistry demonstration comprises six conversations and 18 responses from an unidentified backend served through the free logged out ChatGPT interface in July 2026. Neutral evaluation detected three of five intended deviations. Both initial misses, involving oxidant stoichiometry and experimental scale, were detected at the authority framed second turn; all five detections persisted at the third turn audit. The fixed sequence supports a descriptive account of recovery across turns. In the scale case, the model initially produced a locally coherent peroxide limited yield. After recognizing the unit problem, it incorrectly retained that limiting reagent conclusion for the corrected scale. Detection and numerical repair therefore require separate assessment. The verified reference attracted speculative concerns while retaining its correct yield calculation.

title: Strategies for using Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education considering Ethical Issues, Academic Integrity and Academic Freedom
abstract: This presentation explores strategies for using artificial intelligence in higher education while addressing ethical issues, academic integrity and academic freedom. Drawing on selected research, reported cases and the concept of a post-generative society, it discusses independent learning, human responsibility in peer review, opportunities for discovery and alternatives to personal AI use. It proposes approaches to teaching and governance and synthesises recommendations on intellectual sovereignty into eight action areas, including AI literacy, disciplinary expertise, AI-free learning spaces, assessment, learning research and shared institutional support.

title: Lecturers' perceptions of the benefits and risks of generative Artificial Intelligence [AI] in teaching, learning and assessment: A case of selected universities in Rwanda
abstract: This study investigated lecturers' perceptions of the benefits and risks of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in teaching, learning, and assessment in selected universities in Rwanda. The study was grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) developed by Venkatesh et al., which identifies performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions as the main determinants of technology acceptance and use. UTAUT guided the examination of how lecturers' perceptions of GenAI's usefulness, institutional environment, and potential consequences shape their willingness to integrate it into their practice. The study employed an exploratory qualitative research design. The population comprised university lecturers from five purposively selected universities, including two public and three private institutions. A sample of 40 lecturers, eight from each university, was purposively selected based on their awareness, experience, or exposure to GenAI tools. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analysed thematically using Braun and Clarke's six-phase framework. The findings revealed that lecturers perceived GenAI as both beneficial and risky. Benefits included reduced lesson preparation time, generation of instructional materials and assessment items, alternative explanations, enhanced creativity, personalized learning, and improved feedback. title: Integrating AI Literacy in Any Classroom
abstract: This resource helps educators integrate AI literacy into existing lessons across subject areas. It introduces the Digital Promise AI Literacy Framework and its three modes of engagement: Understand, Evaluate, and Use. Six practices cover data privacy, ethics, digital communication, information integrity, data analysis, and algorithmic thinking. The AI Lesson Design Canvas guides educators in setting academic and AI literacy goals, identifying workforce competencies and credentials, and designing authentic tasks that model responsible AI use. Educators plan evidence, such as AI prompt logs, alongside assessment and reflection. The resource connects AI literacy with durable skills including critical thinking, communication, and decision-making.

title: Developing and validating the human-AI collaboration competency scale
abstract: Abstract Fostering learners’ capacity to collaborate effectively with AI has become an important goal in education. This study aims to develop and validate the Human–AI Collaboration Competency (HACC) Scale, which can be used to assess students’ perceived competency in allocating roles and managing tasks, and sharing, coordinating, and integrating with AI through ongoing interaction to achieve a common goal. This scale includes five constructs’’: engagement, fluency, team bond, interdependence, and task regulation. Two independent samples of high school students were used to examine the factor structures: Sample 1 (n = 195) was used for exploratory factor analysis (EFA), and Sample 2 (n = 356) was used for confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). The final version of the HACC Scale consisted of 25 items loaded onto 5 factors. Construct validity was supported through EFA and CFA, and evidence for convergent validity was obtained by examining the correlations between the measures of digital literacy, AI literacy, AI attitude, and collaborative learning skills. The findings provide empirical support for the internal structure and external associations of the HACC Scale, showing that this scale provides a basis for future research and instructional practices aimed at enhancing human–AI collaboration.

title: Artificial Intelligence Use by University Educators: A Critical Integrative Review Towards a Professionally Situated Conceptualisation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming embedded in higher education teaching, assessment, research and academic support. However, the educational value of AI cannot be adequately explained by the availability of AI tools, frequency of use or technical competence alone. University educators operate within professional, disciplinary, institutional and ethical contexts in which AI generated outputs must be interpreted, evaluated, adapted and sometimes rejected. This article critically integrates recent research on AI use by university educators to develop a professionally situated conceptualization of AI mediated educational practice. The review focuses particularly on educators' patterns of AI use, AI literacy, professional and disciplinary knowledge, human AI interaction, professional judgement, ethical and regulatory accountability, institutional context and reflective professional learning. The synthesis indicates that educators increasingly use AI for preparation of learning materials, generation of activities, feedback, formative assessment, research support and administrative work, but adoption remains selective and context dependent. AI literacy is important but does not by itself ensure educationally appropriate practice. Similarly, institutional policies and professional development influence adoption without determining how educators ultimately use AI. title: AI Literacy Beyond the CS Major: Teaching Staff, Non-Majors, Adults, and Communities
abstract: As institutions scramble to respond to generative AI, computing educators are increasingly asked to teach far beyond their usual classrooms: workshops for university staff, AI-literacy modules for non-majors, faculty development sessions, community and adult-education courses, K-12 outreach, library programming. These audiences differ fundamentally from computing students—in motivation, anxiety, prior mental models, professional stakes, and in what ''literacy'' should even mean for them—yet most of our pedagogical toolkit quietly assumes programmers. This Birds of a Feather convenes everyone doing this work, being asked to do it, or wondering whether they should. The session is organized around three questions, posed here and answered concretely by the room: (1) What does AI literacy mean for the audiences you serve—a registrar, a nurse, a retiree, a ninth-grader, a dean? (2) Which framings and activities land with which audiences, and which reliably flop—including how to address fear and hype in the same room, and wildly mixed prior exposure? (3) What institutional support, credit, and preparation exists for this labor—and what is missing? Participants swap concrete activities, framings, and honest war stories in co-facilitated breakout groups organized by the audiences they serve, and co-construct a shared living grid of activities matched to audiences. title: The Influence of AI Training Programs on Employee Performance: The Mediating Role of Employee Engagement
abstract: The aim of this study was to investigate the impact of AI Training Programs on Employee Performance and Employee Engagement, and to explore the mediating effects of Employee Engagement between AI Training Programs and Employee Performance. With an increasing number of organizations incorporating artificial intelligence technologies, it is crucial to empower workers with proper training to maximize the utilization of the technology and enhance their performance. A structured questionnaire was used for data collection and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was applied for data analysis. The results indicated that AI Training Programs had a significant positive impact on Employee Performance and Employee Engagement. The results also indicated that Employee Engagement positively influenced Employee Performance. In addition, Employee Engagement was found to be statistically significant to mediate the relationship between AI Training Programs and Employee Performance, indicating that AI training programs have an indirect effect on Employee Performance through employee engagement. The results underscore the need for investing in AI training initiatives to build employees' skills, boost engagement levels, and enhance overall job performance. The study adds to the existing literature on the application of AI in HRD and offers valuable insights to organisations looking to optimise AI implementation efforts through employee training and engagement initiatives.

title: AI Literacy Beyond Formal Education: A Week-Long Training for Young Adults
abstract: As AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, AI literacy is no longer relevant only to CS students. However, most AI education initiatives still focus on formal educational settings, leaving many young adults with limited opportunities to develop their AI literacy. In this paper, we present a week-long non-formal AI training designed for 36 young adults aged 18 to 31 from six European countries. The program combined interactive, hands-on activities on AI, with an emphasis on reflection and collaboration. To examine its impact, we collected pre- and post-training assessments on participants' AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, and evaluations of the training. Findings suggest that the training improved awareness of how AI can be used, increased ethical sensitivity, and strengthened overall AI literacy. Participants also reported high levels of engagement, learning, and willingness to participate in further AI-related training. These results highlight the value of non-formal approaches for broadening access to AI education and supporting more inclusive AI literacy development beyond the classroom.

title: From Reporting to Readiness: Governing AI Across the Employee Lifecycle in Manufacturing
abstract: Most HR functions adopt artificial intelligence one tool at a time. In manufacturing, where a missing operator or a lapsed safety certification can stop a production line, the workforce questions that matter most cut across many tools at once. This study develops an integrated approach to AI across the employee lifecycle and a practical way to decide how, and in what order, each use case should be deployed. The study follows a design-science approach. Evidence comes from structured discussions with between 30 and 50 HR practitioners during AI training programs, a documented use-case discovery exercise in the HR function of a manufacturing organization, and a sector extension. Thirteen use cases were mapped for data dependencies and classified against four governance dimensions (data sensitivity, personal data, human review, and system integration) into three deployment tiers. Four use cases were examined in depth. The use cases form an ecosystem rather than a menu: everyday operational tools generate the data that analytical and predictive applications depend on. Only one use case qualified as a low-risk quick win, nine required monitored team deployment, and three (recruitment decisions, skills-to-shift matching, and individual attrition scoring) fell into the highest tier. Practitioners frequently framed success as the removal of human involvement, even when outputs shape decisions about individual people. title: Mapping the Ecosystem of Large Language Models’ Implementation in the Public Sector: A Systematic Evidence Map
abstract: This study examines the implementation of Large Language Models (LLMs) in the public sector through a systematic literature review. Despite growing scholarly attention, existing knowledge remains fragmented, lacking a comprehensive map of empirical evidence. Following PRISMA guidelines, 26 studies from academic databases were analysed using thematic analysis for qualitative synthesis and descriptive statistics to identify patterns across the literature. Four core themes emerged from the analysis: applications of LLMs across government functions; architectures enabling deployment; governance mechanisms shaping implementation; and challenges impeding adoption. Key research trends reveal that scholarly attention concentrates heavily on citizen-facing and policy domains, while operational areas remain underexplored. The field remains in an exploratory phase, with General GenAI/LLM studies dominating compared to enterprise platforms, multi-agent, and multimodal typologies. Internal organisational frameworks emerge as the predominant governance mechanism examined. Technical performance challenges motivate most scholarly inquiry, yet sovereignty and equity concerns appear least often as initial drivers yet recur as barriers in practice. title: Governing Frontier AI: Organizational Boundaries and the Providers of AI Governance
abstract: Who performs the work of frontier-AI governance, and what role do commercial specialists play in it? We combine first-party disclosures from 12 developers with at least one publicly announced model whose training compute is estimated to be above 1025 FLOPs with a frozen Crunchbase-derived classifier of commercial AI-governance providers. A systematic verification pass yields 238 realized model- or system-specific governance-provision instances across 10 developers. Collapsing repeated model-level observations produces 99 unique developer–provider/process–function relationships, of which 58 cross an organizational boundary. Evaluation is the most frequently documented function, accounting for 53 of 99 relationships and spanning internal, for-profit/certification, public, nonprofit/research, and unnamed external modes. External evidence remains highly concentrated: OpenAI and Anthropic account for 50 of 58 external relationships. Because the evidence is disclosure-dependent and based primarily on English-language public sources, this concentration should not be read as a population measure of outsourcing. On the commercial side, the frozen classifier identifies 51 canonical specialist firms, 25 of which have positive disclosed funding amounts. These firms have approximately $428.5 million in disclosed historical funding, with 85.3% concentrated in the ten largest. title: Too Big to Inspect? Ethically Auditing Large Datasets Through Small Samples
abstract: Big techs and researchers increasingly claim that their training datasets are too large to inspect for bias and ethical problems. However, in the race to build ever-large models, they have relied on automated web scraping and no human curation. Datasets built this way absorb the stereotypes, exclusionary norms, and historical prejudices of their sources, and the models trained on them can reproduce and amplify those patterns. Because manually auditing billions of samples is humanly impossible, we need practical, effective methods to identify biases in these datasets. This paper studies the feasibility of ethically auditing large datasets through small samples and proposes a practical method for identifying structural biases by applying AI Ethics Tools (AIETs) to random samples. We applied Datasheets for Datasets, Data Statements, Data Nutrition Labels, and Data Cards to a 1% sample of Framed Multi30K, and Datasheets for Datasets to two 0.00006% samples of relaion2B-en-research-safe. Our results show that evaluating small samples with AIETs can reveal ethical problems, structural biases, and technical inconsistencies. Although industry practice assumes that identifying problems requires analyzing the entire dataset, we show that a random subset supports a viable qualitative analysis without overwhelming computational or human resources. title: The “Beijing Effect” in AI Regulation
abstract: In this paper, the author analyzes the concept of the “Beijing effect” as an alternative to the concept of “digital authoritarianism”. The relevance of the topic stems from the rapid growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) sector and the emergence of various models of its regulation. The paper also analyzes the concept of the Digital Silk Road as a tool through which investments in the economies of other countries are transformed into China’s political influence. The author concludes that there is a transition from hard “lock-in” to soft influence, facilitated by standards and open AI models. The paper shows how China, by financing the digital infrastructure of developing countries, renders their digital sovereignty illusory. The work is valuable for understanding why AI regulation cannot be reduced to laws when the underlying infrastructure is owned by other countries.

title: Hardness of AI Regulation Shapes
abstract: Governments now regulate artificial intelligence with very different degrees of legal force. Yet we know little about how this shapes academics. In this article, I ask how the hardness of AI regulation shapes academic competence. I compare Hungary, Japan and Bangladesh, which represent mandated, encouraged and drafted regulatory regimes respectively. Instruments were coded, and studies were reviewed. Coding followed obligation, precision, delegation and reach, and screening followed PRISMA 2020. Hungary ranked highest, yet Bangladesh trailed behind. Japan sat between them, and guidance filled gaps. Hard law widened the coverage of staff training, yet it rewarded documentation more than pedagogical depth or critical judgement. Soft guidance multiplied institutional guidelines, and their quality varied considerably. Bangladeshi rules remained drafts, so lecturers largely taught themselves through informal, unsupported experimentation. I propose that competence depth peaks not under the hardest statutes but where moderate obligation meets precise direction and capable support bodies. What follows are five testable propositions. The article offers policymakers, quality agencies and faculty developers a comparative vocabulary for designing AI competence frameworks. It also explains why softening the EU's literacy duty now matters.

title: AI Transformative Law: The Urgency and Direction of AI Regulation in Indonesia
abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in Indonesia has expanded rapidly, while the national legal framework remains fragmented across general laws governing electronic information and personal data, as well as nonbinding ethical guidelines. This regulatory mismatch creates uncertainty regarding AI risk classification, accountability, transparency, and oversight. Objective: This study examines the urgency and direction of AI regulation in Indonesia and evaluates its emerging legal character through the theoretical perspectives of responsive law, progressive law, and transformative law. Methods: This normative juridical study employs a statutory approach to examine primary, secondary, and tertiary legal materials. The materials are analyzed descriptively and qualitatively, using the three legal perspectives as analytical frameworks. The analytical indicators include responsiveness to social needs, human-centered legal change, future-oriented regulatory steering, reliance on technical expertise, and cross-sectoral governance. Results: Indonesia’s two draft presidential regulations on the National AI Roadmap and AI Ethics and Governance constitute an initial framework for cross-sectoral governance rather than a comprehensive and binding legal regime. title: AI Governance: A Comparative Economic Analysis of Japanese and Indonesian AI Regulation
abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has prompted global discourse on the need for a robust regulatory framework that addresses ethical, legal, and social issues and fosters the innovation through the efficiencies created by AI. This research conducts a comparative analysis of the AI governance frameworks in Japan and Indonesia, examined through the theoretical lens of Economic Analysis of Law (EAL). Japan has taken a nuanced approach that balances the dynamic development of AI with ethical oversight to uphold the Human-Centered AI Social Principles. Indonesia is in the formative stages of developing its AI regulatory environment. Through EAL, this research assesses the efficiency implications of the AI regulatory frameworks between Japan and Indonesia, looking at the implementation of AI in society. By comparing these approaches, this paper highlights the challenges and opportunities for Indonesia in regulating AI technology for the public interest. Indonesia is advised to take a multi-stakeholder approach to build consensus and engage in bilateral cooperation with Japan for the establishment of domestic legislation. title: Compliance, Data Security, Law and Ethical AI Regulation in Decentralized Approached Using TinyML
abstract: TinyML, which enables to execute ML models on low-energy-consuming devices, is already applied in a broad variety of environments, such as intelligent homes, medicine, and cars. The use of TinyML in processing personal information is on the rise, and this raises privacy, governance, and AI regulations. In this paper, we explained the moral and legal consequences of TinyML, and why good practice should be applied in regard to data privacy, transparency, accountability, and fairness of ML computer programs. Having the privacy laws such as the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance is a challenge to making use of TinyML, due to the fact that the data is processed at the edge devices. This causes data security, consent, and privacy problems. And, as AI legislation exists (such as the AI act proposed by the European Union), AI systems will have to be socially acceptable and responsible. TinyML ML models have many ethical issues, including biased data and AI decision-making and consequences to employment and human rights. This is why there is a necessity of some ethical principles incorporated into TinyML development process to guarantee the protection of human rights and prevent harm. Another study has also concluded that there is a need of governance, data protection, and best practices in the deployment of TinyML systems regarding the legal and ethical aspects.

title: Unstable ground: Automated dialect recognition, ground truth, and AI regulation in asylum procedures
abstract: Abstract While problems of AI systems are often attributed to technical shortcomings, some systems fail because they are built on ontologically and epistemologically “unstable ground.” Ground truth, or the datasets against which machine-learning systems are trained, validated, and tested, renders a particular representation of the world learnable by translating complex qualitative phenomena into mathematical formalisms. In doing so, it can stabilize tenuous truth claims while concealing fundamental flaws in how those phenomena are modeled, leaving systems unable to address the problems they are designed to solve. We examine this problem through a case study of Germany’s Dialect Identification Assistance System (DIAS), an automated language assessment system used in determining asylum applicants’ countries of origin. Drawing on Ground Truth Tracing (Kang 2023), we identify three reductions through which DIAS links speech to country of origin: treating language as code, mapping dialect onto bounded territory, and inferring nationality from this mapping. From linguistic and legal perspectives, these assumptions lack sufficient empirical grounding. DIAS may therefore produce internally coherent outputs while lacking the capacity to fulfil its intended task. title: Discursive Manipulation of National Security and Industrial Competitiveness in U.S. AI Regulation: Domestic Contestation and the Fragmentation of Global AI Governance
abstract: Against the backdrop of generative AI emerging as a core strategic asset for major powers, the rhetorical tropes of national security and industrial competitiveness are subject to strategic manipulation by divergent domestic actors. The deregulatory camp within the White House invokes industrial competitiveness to roll back security-focused executive orders; the security faction in Congress expands chip export controls in the name of national defense; state-level authorities counter federal overreach through consumer protection mandates; and Silicon Valley deploys a two-pronged lobbying strategy. Taking the 2023-2026 policy pendulum and BIS chip regulations as its analytical case, this paper demonstrates that domestic contestation spills over globally through transmission channels. This has produced a global AI governance landscape defined by fragmentation, hollowed-out soft law processes, and a three-bloc divide across the U.S., the EU, and China, while the shortening commitment half-life of U.S. policy positions has inflated the costs of multilateral cooperation. The study also identifies limited positive spillover effects. In response, the paper puts forward targeted strategies. The conclusion argues that U.S. internal regulatory divisions constitute a mechanism that externalizes domestic political costs as global governance uncertainty. Understanding this mechanism is a prerequisite for reshaping the multilateral AI order.

title: REGULATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN FINTECH SECTOR: CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES IN INDONESIA
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly influenced various sectors, including financial technology (fintech). In Indonesia, fintech innovations such as digital payments and wealth management are reshaping financial services. However, the regulatory framework for AI in this sector remains underdeveloped, creating both challenges and opportunities. This article explores the current state of AI regulation in Indonesia's fintech sector and examines the potential hurdles and benefits of implementing comprehensive AI regulations. Utilizing a normative juridical approach, the study integrates conceptual, statutory, and case-based analyses to provide a multidimensional understanding of the issue. The findings reveal several challenges, including algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, and the complexity of ensuring transparency and accountability in AI-based decision-making. On the other hand, AI offers opportunities for increased efficiency, enhanced risk assessment, and improved financial services scalability. The article underscores the urgency of establishing specific regulations to ensure AI accountability and transparency while fostering innovation. Such measures will help Indonesia balance the benefits of AI integration in fintech with the need to safeguard legal and ethical standards.

title: Risk-based ai regulatory reconstruction for legal certainty and digital rights protection in Indonesia
abstract: This study examines Indonesia's AI regulatory position through normative legal research, comparative regulatory analysis, and quantitative analysis of the AI Regulation Map using a 13 June 2026 snapshot. The comparison covers Indonesia and seven comparator jurisdictions, Singapore, South Korea, Japan, Spain, Italy, Sweden, and the United States, across Regulation Status, Policy Lever, Governance Type, Actor Involvement, and Enforcement Level. The findings indicate that Indonesia has lower scores than the comparator mean on the three normative dimensions used by the AI Regulation Map's Maturity Index, with gaps of 2.29 points for Regulation Status, 1.93 points for Policy Lever, and 1.54 points for Enforcement Level. Because the map is a derived indicator rather than a direct legal-validity or enforcement measure, the results are interpreted as comparative regulatory signals and are cross-checked against Indonesian and comparator primary legal sources. The normative reconstruction proposes a legal architecture that distinguishes enacted rules from guidance and draft instruments, classifies AI by risk, assigns proportionate obligations to relevant actors, embeds human oversight and digital-rights safeguards, and connects supervision with incident reporting, sanctions, and individual remedies.

title: Regulation
abstract: This chapter traces broad trends in the legal and socio-legal literature that discussed the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) regulation since the turn of the century. It applies Ayres and Braithwaite’s responsive regulation framework, with a focus on its distinctive ‘pyramid of regulatory strategies’, to shed new light on trends in the behaviour of AI developers and concomitant regulatory responses. The chapter shows that the development of regulation in respect of data and AI over time broadly correlates with the escalating interventions depicted in the regulatory pyramid. These responses can be categorised into four broad stages: (i) early industry self-regulation (2000–2010), (ii) data protection regulations (2010–2015), (iii) ethics-focused soft regulation as the regulatory focus shifted from Big Data to AI (2015–2024), and (iv) the emergence of variants of command-and-control AI legislation in some jurisdictions accompanied by deregulatory pressures in others (2024 onwards). The chapter’s analysis reveals general trends towards increasingly interventionist responses to industry conduct and behaviour across diverse jurisdictions, initially in response to Big Data and then in response to AI as regulatory targets. It concludes by outlining ongoing challenges for AI regulation as regulators continually try to respond to, or catch up with, problems as they become apparent.

abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how ethical concerns about open-source artificial intelligence (AI) artefacts become publicly sustained and incorporated into documentation, with implications for health-care organisations procuring and governing components they did not build. The corpus comprises 450 keyword-retained issue threads and 2,136 within-window comments, analysed through Big Q reflexive thematic analysis, a transparent marker audit and cross-case pattern matching. Findings Fairlearn repeatedly converts data set, terminology, intended-use and metric-interpretation debates into documentation. abstract: This exploratory study examines artificial intelligence anxiety among academic librarians in the United Arab Emirates, a multilingual context undergoing rapid digital transformation. title: Responsible AI in Public Health Systems: Governance Principles and an Implementation Model for Indian States
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering Indian public health systems through screening tools, clinical decision support, disease surveillance, health-record analytics and citizen-facing chatbots. State health departments, which run most public facilities, are often the buyers and operators of these tools, yet they have limited guidance on how to evaluate, procure, deploy and monitor them responsibly. International and national guidance — including the World Health Organization's guidance on the ethics and governance of AI for health and the Indian Council of Medical Research's ethical guidelines for AI in biomedical research and healthcare — sets out principles, but translating them into state-level practice remains a gap. This paper proposes an implementation model for responsible AI in state public health systems, organised around the AI life cycle: need and problem definition; data governance; evaluation and validation; procurement; deployment and workflow integration; monitoring and incident management; and decommissioning. It pairs each stage with governance principles, minimum requirements and responsible roles, and recommends an institutional structure — a state AI-in-health committee supported by a technical assessment cell. The paper draws on published guidance and research and on the author's experience in state digital health programmes; it is a policy and implementation framework, not an empirical study.

title: Responsible AI in Public-Serving Institutions: Advances, Challenges, and Future Directions
abstract: Public-serving institutions (government agencies, courts, health systems, social-welfare bodies, and regulators) are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) to triage caseloads, allocate resources, detect fraud, and personalize services. Because these institutions exercise coercive and distributive authority over citizens who cannot easily exit the relationship, the stakes of getting AI wrong are qualitatively different from those in commercial settings. This paper surveys the advances, challenges, and future directions of responsible AI in the public sector, synthesizing scholarship on AI in government, algorithmic fairness, transparency, and AI ethics with practitioner-facing governance instruments. We first delimit what makes public-serving institutions distinctive: statutory mandates, due-process obligations, and diffuse accountability. We then map the state of the art across four dimensions (use cases, governance and policy instruments, fairness/transparency/accountability practices, and organizational capacity and procurement) and consolidate representative advances in a described table. We argue that the field has matured from principle proliferation toward operational risk management, exemplified by the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the OECD AI Principles, yet a persistent gap remains between high-level commitments and verifiable practice on the ground. title: Human likeness is a misplaced benchmark for artificial intelligence
abstract: Recent claims that large language models pass the Turing test span different procedures, but share a common focus on human outputs, rather than the processes that lead to those outputs. Here we challenge the inference from successful imitation to intelligence. Similar outputs can arise from different processes and conceal differences in reasoning, generalization, and adaptation. More fundamentally, we question whether human likeness should guide AI development at all. Prioritizing imitation can reproduce human biases, facilitate manipulation, and favor replacing people over augmenting their capabilities. AI systems should expand human welfare, not merely impersonate us. We recommend three coordinated changes: designing systems that strengthen human capabilities and independent judgment; requiring funded projects to assess benefits, costs, and their distribution; and guiding institutional procurement and renewal by evidence of AI’s effects on human welfare.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Socialist Rule-of-Law State in Vietnam: Rethinking the Exercise and Control of Public Power
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly entering public administration and governmental decision-making, expanding state capacity while raising new questions about the exercise and control of public power. This article examines these questions from the perspective of Vietnam's socialist rule-of-law State. It argues that AI is not a new source or autonomous subject of state power, but a technological condition through which legally constituted public authority may increasingly be exercised. The article develops the concept of the AI-mediated exercise of public power, referring to situations in which AI materially shapes the informational, analytical, procedural, or decisional processes through which public authorities make consequential decisions. Building on people's sovereignty, legality, state-power control, and accountability, it advances an Extension Thesis: when AI materially mediates public authority, effective control of state power must extend to the data, algorithms, AI systems, and human–AI arrangements through which that authority is exercised. The article further develops meaningful human authority and a public-power extension of existing AI impact-assessment arrangements. It concludes that AI-enabled modernization requires corresponding modernization of the institutions through which public power is authorized, exercised, controlled, and held accountable to the People.

abstract: Managing operational staff in police forces, military corporations and government security agencies is one of the most difficult structural problems in public administration. Reliance on fragmented legacy systems and static spreadsheets leads to poor administrative transparency, slow troop mobilization, errors in calculating entitlements and regulatory time off, higher overtime costs, and physical and psychological strain on officers. This paper proposes a conceptual and architectural model of Predictive Workforce Governance that combines cloud computing (SaaS/IaaS), data science, and predictive and generative artificial intelligence (AI). The model is organized in three layers: (i) cloud data ingestion and automation, which centralizes and standardizes availability, payroll and specialized tactical skills data (such as snipers, pilots, tactical drivers and crisis negotiators); (ii) analytics and prediction, using statistical and machine learning models (ARIMA and seasonal multiple regression) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to anticipate staffing gaps, simulate demand peaks during critical events and detect early signs of fatigue and operational stress; and (iii) decision interface and visualization, with real-time management dashboards built around a Troop Readiness Index (TRI). title: Perils and opportunities of AI for public climate services
abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative and machine-learning systems, in climate services development and provision is transforming how climate information is produced, accessed, and interpreted. AI-enabled climate services offer significant opportunities for process automation, optimisation, tailoring, and the translation of complex climate data into actionable knowledge for diverse users. However, the growing reliance on privately controlled algorithms, data infrastructures, and computing facilities raises critical concerns related to governance, transparency, equity and economic sustainability, among others. While the technical architecture of climate services increasingly relies on advanced machine learning and large-scale climate models, their legitimacy as public services may be weakened in the absence of arrangements that prioritise public value and long-lasting societal benefit over profit maximisation. The tension between the public mandate of climate services and the private nature of AI infrastructure challenges traditional notions of openness. Using a consensus-based elicitation method coupled with the PESTLE framework, we analyse the political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental risks and opportunities shaping the co-production value chain of AI-enabled climate services. title: A co-production approach to resilience thinking operationalisation in disaster risk reduction
abstract: This article examines how resilience thinking can be operationalised through a co-production with stakeholders in the disaster risk reduction sector (DRR). Through transdisciplinary research within the national context of Czechia, this study addresses the general gap between resilience as a widely promoted theoretical concept and the challenges of its practical implementation. The research process involved two participatory workshops with DRR stakeholders from public administration, research, NGOs, emergency services, local governments, volunteering, and communities affected by disasters. Workshop data and co-produced materials were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis, guided by the seven resilience thinking principles. Rather than reducing operationalisation to indicators, our approach shows how resilience principles can be operationalised through the co-production of shared visions and concrete pathways that reflect the realities of DRR systems. Resulting visions and pathways include dimensions that are often difficult to capture through indicator-focused resilience operationalisation – e.g., local and tacit knowledge, social and institutional barriers, power relations or cultural context. This co-productive approach shifts the focus from measuring resilience to enacting it and integrates multiple epistemologies into the operationalisation process. title: Transdisciplinary spaces for co-production: facilitating climate action in smaller municipalities through creating transformation knowledge
abstract: Abstract Smaller municipalities face numerous challenges in pursuing climate action, including the modernization of public buildings. Since buildings account for around 30% of CO 2 emissions, they offer significant leverage. Structural barriers like limited funding and a lack of qualified personnel often hinder implementation – even when awareness, political will, and clarity on potential measures exist. This highlights that systems knowledge (facts) and target knowledge (norms and values) are insufficient without transformation knowledge (action-oriented knowledge). This article explores how small municipalities can develop transformation knowledge through co-production processes. Using a longitudinal study, we demonstrate the importance of trusted spaces for open dialog and scientific support to translate ideas into practical solutions. Transdisciplinary approaches, such as the three-phase model, are shown to effectively empower municipalities. By collaboratively developing tailored solutions, municipalities can overcome barriers and engage in impactful climate action, as demonstrated in a case study of municipalities in the German state of Hesse.

title: Decision Rights, Responsibilities, and Disagreement Resolution in Patient Involvement and Co-production: A Scoping Review and Comparative Documentary Analysis
abstract: Research Project Description Patient involvement, shared decision-making, and co-production are increasingly emphasized in healthcare policy and practice. However, these approaches raise important questions about the allocation of decision-making authority, the respective responsibilities of patients and healthcare professionals, and the processes available for resolving disagreements over treatment decisions. This research aims to systematically examine how existing legal, ethical, professional, regulatory, and accreditation frameworks define and integrate these decision rights, responsibilities, and disagreement-resolution arrangements. Particular attention will be given to patients' rights to participate in decisions, request or refuse treatment, healthcare professionals' authority and obligations when declining requests considered clinically inappropriate, nurses' responsibilities for advocacy and escalation, and organizational mechanisms for resolving disagreements while maintaining continuity of care. The study will examine frameworks from five jurisdictions: the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Australia, alongside relevant guidance from the World Health Organization and international professional bodies. It will consider both individual clinical encounters and patient involvement in healthcare service design, quality improvement, and organizational governance. title: Understanding and enhancing co-production in climate litigation: Trends and gaps in synergies between civil society, law and science
abstract: In the current context of insufficient climate action and unmet demands for climate justice, civil society organizations are increasingly turning to the courts as part of a broader repertoire of strategies to accelerate ecological transitions and drive systemic change. This has contributed to a global surge in climate litigation, manifested through diverse legal arguments and associated campaigns. Climate litigation frequently leads litigants to combine advocacy and activism with legal opportunities and scientific evidence, both inside and outside the courtroom. These practical and epistemic synergies across social, legal and scientific domains, and their implications, are the focus of this empirical study. Based on twenty-four in-depth interviews with a globally distributed sample of litigants and experts, we document emerging trends in collaborations between civil society, law, and science, as well as gaps that, if addressed, could enhance their collective impact. Drawing on theories of legal mobilization, co-production and sustainability transitions, we clarify the boundary work in which litigants are engaged to influence climate governance while extending the research frontier toward the political and epistemic dimensions of climate litigation. We conceptualize these interactions as the co-production of climate litigation – an analytical lens and strategic mechanism to trace how collaborations feed into wider sustainability transitions. title: Co-production of eENHANCE: a web platform to deliver personalised nutrition and exercise support to prevent cancer-related malnutrition and muscle loss
abstract: PURPOSE: Access to nutrition and exercise services for people with cancer-related malnutrition varies across health services. This study co-produced a personalised self-guided evidence-based nutrition and exercise web program and evaluated feasibility and acceptability within clinical practice. METHODS: A co-production approach was utilised following the four phases of Design Thinking in Healthcare. Phase 1 gathered user needs through interviews with consumers and health professionals, which were analysed using thematic analysis. Solutions were generated in Phase 2 to inform content and development of the platform. Phase 3 involved user acceptance testing. Feasibility testing in a clinical setting was undertaken in Phase 4. RESULTS: Phase 1: interviews with 14 health professionals (100% female, mean age 59.5 [range 25-57] years) and five people with cancer (100% female, mean age 53.5 [range 57-62] years) generated three themes: (1) patient characteristics, (2) features and functions of the web platform and (3) optimising practice. Phase 2: an 8-week evidence-based self-guided nutrition and exercise program (eENHANCE) was developed based on the interview findings and refined in Phase 3 testing. Phase 4: 20 people with cancer participated in feasibility testing of eENHANCE at a tertiary cancer centre, with high (86%) acceptability of the intervention, compliance with study outcome assessment (67-100%), while 30-100% accessed prescribed modules. title: Co-Production of Nattokinase and Menaquinone-7 by Bacillus subtilis Natto: Metabolic Trade-Offs, Regulatory Mechanisms, and Dynamic Fermentation Strategies
abstract: Bacillus subtilis natto can co-produce nattokinase (NK) and menaquinone-7 (MK-7), but their distinct biosynthetic demands, cellular localization, and production kinetics may be associated with condition-dependent trade-offs. This review critically evaluates the biosynthetic mechanisms and multi-omics regulatory characteristics of NK and MK-7 and examines how oxygen-related conditions, substrate composition, and redox state are associated with co-production performance. Dynamic two-stage fermentation has been proposed as a promising, system-dependent framework for coordinating the different production phases of NK and MK-7. However, current evidence remains limited to specific strains, substrates, and reactor configurations. Future studies should integrate 13C metabolic flux analysis, real-time sensing, standardized detection, and non-GM strain improvement to drive NK-MK-7 co-production from empirical optimization toward mechanism-driven predictive design, providing a theoretical and technical basis for dual-functional foods and multi-product fermentation.
